rows.title: Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003): for first-passage percolation on Z^d with d > 1 whose edge weights are i.i.d. and TWO-VALUED - omega_e equal to a or to b with probability 1/2 each, for fixed 0 < a < b < infinity - the distance from the origin to a vertex v with |v| > 2 satisfies Var dist_omega(0,v) <= C |v| / log |v|, where C = C(a,b,d). The theorem as published is NOT a general-distribution result: the symmetric two-point law is a hypothesis, not an illustration.
rows.body:
d > 1
edge weights i.i.d., taking exactly two values a and b, each with probability exactly 1/2
0 < a < b < infinity fixed
|v| > 2

THE HYPOTHESIS THAT GETS DROPPED IN QUOTATION: the symmetric two-point (Bernoulli a/b) law is load-bearing. The survey records why: 'This specific distribution was needed to take advantage of Talagrand's influence inequality on the hypercube.' Any statement of the form 'BKS proved sublinear variance for FPP' without the two-point qualifier is a misquotation of the 2003 paper; the general-distribution version is Damron-Hanson-Sosoe, a decade later.
CONSTANT DEPENDENCE: C depends only on a, b and d - not on v and not on the direction.
VERSION TRAP: the arXiv comment on v5 reads 'Replaced theorem 2 (which was incorrect) by a new theorem'. Cite v5 or the journal version; a citation resolved to an earlier version can carry a withdrawn Theorem 2.
SOURCE: arXiv:math/0203262v5; Ann. Probab. 31 (2003), 1970-1978. (The arXiv journal-ref field prints '31:197-1978', a typo for 1970-1978; the survey bibliography gives 1970-1978.) Hypothesis set read in the authors' own abstract, and corroborated in Auffinger-Damron-Hanson, '50 years of first passage percolation', arXiv:1511.03262v2 (AMS University Lecture Series 68, 2017), tex line 1170, and in the abstract of arXiv:2604.01214 ('...used hypercontractivity to obtain an improvement of a factor of log n when passage times take two values with equal probability').
VERIFICATION STATUS: theorem-checked-against-source. The v5 abstract states the hypotheses, the conclusion and the constant dependence in full; the proof was not read.

rows.title: Open problem: Benjamini-Schramm conjecture: p_c < p_u if and only if the group is non-amenable
rows.body:
OPEN PROBLEM (source_says_open; current status unverified; result status attempted_unsolved). For a Cayley graph G of a finitely generated infinite group, p_c(G) < p_u(G) if and only if the group is non-amenable. Source: Duminil-Copin: Sixty years of percolation, ICM 2018, Conjecture 2, p. 4. Status notes: Amenable direction is known (Burton-Keane uniqueness gives p_c = p_u). The non-amenable direction is known for many classes (Pak-Smirnova for some generating sets, Hutchcroft for several classes including nonunimodular and hyperbolic settings); not verified in a bounded search whether the full conjecture has been settled by 2026.
Posed in Duminil-Copin: Sixty years of percolation, ICM 2018
Current status unverified as of 2026-09-07

rows.title: Attempt on Benjamini-Schramm conjecture: p_c < p_u if and only if the group is non-amenable
rows.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt the non-amenable direction through the spectral radius criterion of Benjamini-Schramm and Hutchcroft's p_c <= 1/spectral radius... type bounds. Result: Known route: if p_c < 1/rho where rho is the spectral radius of simple random walk, then at p slightly above p_c the expected number of open paths of length n to distance n grows slower than the number of returns... this gives p_c < p_u for graphs where p_c(G) < 1/(rho ... ) and is the content of the Benjamini-Schramm 1996 criterion p_c < 1/(1 + spectral gap)?; the general conjecture needs p_c < p_u even when p_c is close to 1/rho... For groups with p_c(G) < 1/rho(G) the conjecture holds; the remaining case is groups with a Cayley graph where p_c >= 1/rho, and the Pak-Smirnova trick replaces the generating set to make p_c small relative to rho. So the conjecture in its generating-set-free form (some Cayley graph) is settled by Pak-Smirnova, while the conjecture for EVERY Cayley graph reduces to showing p_c(G) < 1/rho(G)^{?}... I checked the inequality p_c <= 1/(1 + h) where h is the Cheeger constant... Benjamini-Schramm prove p_c <= 1/(1+h) and p_u >= 1/(1+h)?? no. The honest reduction: for every Cayley graph, p_c < p_u would follow from p_c < 1/rho (Benjamini-Schramm criterion) and the open question is whether every non-amenable Cayley graph satisfies p_c < 1/rho, which fails? For the free group with the standard generators p_c = 1/(2d-1) and 1/rho = (2d-1)/(2 sqrt(2d-1)) > p_c, consistent. No counterexample and no proof. Obstruction: Need p_c(G) < 1/rho(G) or another uniform criterion for every Cayley graph of every non-amenable group.

rows.title: Technique: Efron-Stein Inequality and the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm Influence Bound
rows.body:
TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Efron-Stein: for f(X_1,...,X_n) with independent coordinates, Var f <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^{(i)}))^2], where X^{(i)} resamples coordinate i; for a Boolean function under a product measure the right side is a constant times the total influence sum_i I_i(f). This bounds variance by total influence and needs no monotonicity. Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (1999): if f_n : {0,1}^{m_n} -> {0,1} satisfy sum_i I_i(f_n)^2 -> 0 then (f_n) is noise sensitive, i.e. Cov(f_n(omega), f_n(omega^eps)) -> 0 for every fixed noise level eps > 0; for monotone functions the converse also holds. The quantitative engine is Talagrand's inequality Var f <= C sum_i I_i(f)/log(e/I_i(f)) (hypercontractivity), which for functions with all influences at most n^{-a} improves Efron-Stein by a factor log n; the same mechanism gives the BKS sublinear variance bound Var(first-passage time to distance n) <= C n/log n for first-passage percolation with suitable edge weights. What these do NOT give: a lower bound on any individual influence (that is Kahn-Kalai-Linial: max_i I_i >= c Var(f) log n / n), or a power improvement n^{1-eps} on the variance, which remains open outside integrable models. Typical failure: Using the plain Efron-Stein variance bound and mistaking it for the BKS lower bound on the maximal individual influence, which is a distinct and much sharper statement requiring monotonicity and a total-influence hypothesis; conflating the two leads to claiming individual-coordinate sensitivity conclusions, needed for noise-sensitivity theorems, from a tool that in its basic form only controls the aggregate variance. Canonical reference: Efron and Stein, 1981, The Annals of Statistics; Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm, 1999, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES.
Independent coordinates (product measure)
BKS noise sensitivity criterion: sum of squared influences tends to zero
Talagrand's logarithmic improvement needs hypercontractivity of the product measure
